name: Community Improvement Project Proposal
description: A warm neighborhood-led proposal system with resident stories, forest-green civic structure, terracotta emphasis, accessible maps, transparent budgets, and participation-focused impact measures.
style_guide:
# Community Improvement Project Proposal

## Visual concept

This English-language style is designed for neighborhood initiatives, public-space improvements, community hubs, safety programs, and resident-led service proposals. It should feel welcoming, grounded, and publicly accountable: warm paper backgrounds create familiarity, deep green signals stewardship, terracotta adds human energy, and candid resident imagery keeps the proposal connected to daily life. Every page should translate community evidence into a practical choice—what residents need, what will be built, who is responsible, where the money goes, and how people can participate.

## Canvas, grid, and safe area

- Use a fixed `1280 x 720 px` canvas in a 16:9 ratio.
- Keep `64–76 px` safe margins on all sides. A cover photograph may bleed to the top, right, and bottom edges, but all type stays inside the safe area.
- Use a 12-column grid with `18–22 px` gutters. Typical layouts are 5/7 title-plus-photo, 6/6 evidence-plus-story, three equal goal cards, 5/7 map-plus-programs, and 7/5 partner-table-plus-budget.
- Reserve a compact running header for a short terracotta rule, section number, chapter name, and page count. Place source notes or reporting context along the bottom edge.
- Set the main headline in the upper quarter and keep `24–36 px` between it and the primary exhibit.
- Align card edges, map frames, timeline markers, table columns, and KPI blocks to shared guides. Use `18–24 px` gaps between modules.
- Keep generous open space around resident quotations and decision statements. Do not crowd public-facing information into a dense administrative layout.

## Color system

### Core colors

- Community paper: `#F4EEE3`. Use as the dominant canvas.
- Civic green: `#2E5845`. Use for stewardship panels, resident principles, secondary data, map markers, and the impact-page background.
- Terracotta: `#C95A3A`. Use for italic headline phrases, active bars, numbered markers, primary goals, and calls to action.
- Neighborhood ink: `#1D1D1B`. Use for titles, body emphasis, table labels, and primary values.
- Clean white: `#FFFFFF`. Use for cards, chart fields, program rows, and light type on Civic green.

### Supporting colors

- Garden sage: `#7E916F`. Use for green-space, local-hiring, or supporting allocation categories.
- Warm clay: `#D89A69`. Use for a third budget segment or human-scale accent.
- Sand: `#C9BFA9`. Use for map streets, inactive bars, dividers, and quiet table bands.
- Body gray: `#68645F`. Use for explanations, metadata, and source notes.

### Usage rules

- Community paper, Civic green, and Terracotta define the visual identity. Keep most pages light and reserve the full green field for the impact or participation page.
- Use Terracotta for one primary emphasis per page: an italic phrase, priority bar, map route, milestone, or next-step block.
- Use Civic green for community ownership and durable infrastructure. Use Terracotta for urgency, activation, or the proposed path.
- Limit a page to three saturated colors and directly label all budget or status categories.
- Do not introduce cool corporate blues, neon accents, gradients, or decorative color coding unrelated to meaning.

## Typography

- Primary font: `Inter`, `Aptos`, or `Helvetica Neue`; fallback: `Arial, system-ui, sans-serif`.
- Use a bold sans serif for conclusion-led headlines and a true italic from the same family for the Terracotta phrase.
- Cover title: `66–90 px`, weight `700–850`, line-height `0.94–1.02`; keep the title to three short lines.
- Content headline: `40–54 px`, weight `700–850`, line-height `1.02–1.12`; one short phrase may appear in Terracotta italic.
- Section label: `10–13 px`, weight `700`, uppercase with `2.5–4 px` tracking, Civic green.
- Hero metric: `40–62 px`, weight `700–850`; keep units visibly attached but smaller.
- Card number: `44–64 px`, italic, using Terracotta or Civic green.
- Card title: `18–24 px`, weight `700–800`.
- Body copy: `13–17 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.4–1.55`.
- Table headers, sources, captions, and page numbers: `9–12 px`, weight `500–700`.
- Use plain, direct language. Avoid bureaucratic jargon, unexplained acronyms, and long all-caps statements.

## Layout and components

- Cards use Clean white, square or nearly square corners, an optional `1 px` Sand border, and no drop shadow.
- Resident-needs bars place the concern on the left, a direct percentage on the right, and a thick Terracotta or Civic green progress bar below. Keep the source within the same card.
- Testimonial panels use Civic green with Community paper text, a large Terracotta quotation mark, and compact attribution. Use only verified, permitted resident wording.
- Goal cards use a `4–5 px` colored top rail, a large two-digit number, one concrete outcome statement, and one measurable definition.
- Principle bands use a full-width Civic green field divided into four equal columns with fine light separators.
- Service-plan pages pair a simple neighborhood map with three stacked program cards. Reuse lettered markers consistently between map and cards.
- Partner tables rely on aligned text and whitespace rather than full cell borders. Highlight the total row with a pale sand field.
- Budget bars use one horizontal 100-percent stack with direct category labels. Timelines use a thin rule and no more than five milestone nodes.
- Participation lists use numbered circles, concise action titles, and one sentence explaining the level of commitment.

## Charts and data

- Prefer ranked bars, KPI cards, simple neighborhood maps, proportional budget bars, milestone timelines, and goal-versus-measure tables.
- Terracotta marks urgent resident needs, proposed investment, or an active milestone; Civic green marks durable community assets, participation, or positive outcomes.
- Show the survey base, collection period, geography, source, and unit with every resident-needs chart.
- Budget exhibits must reconcile to the stated total and distinguish cash, in-kind support, restricted funding, reserve, and estimated amounts.
- Timelines should show permitting, procurement, resident review, construction, launch, measurement, and handover where relevant. Label dates as planned or confirmed.
- Impact metrics require a baseline, target, reporting period, responsible owner, and review cadence. Use targets rather than presenting future results as achieved facts.
- Keep charts directly labeled and accessible. Do not rely on color alone; pair colors with category names, values, letters, or positions.

## Page variations

- Cover: a 5/7 split with a large stacked proposal title on Community paper and an edge-to-edge resident or neighborhood photograph on the right. Add a small civic badge and compact prepared-by metadata.
- Community issue and resident needs: one ranked concern chart beside a large resident quotation and three demographic or reach cards.
- Project goals and design principles: three equal goal cards across the upper body and a four-column Civic green principle band below.
- Activities, facilities, and services: a simple project-footprint map on the left and three stacked location or program cards on the right.
- Partners, budget, and timeline: a partner-contribution table on the left, then a proportional budget bar and five-step delivery timeline on the right.
- Expected impact and participation: a large Civic green KPI field paired with a light participation column and one clear Terracotta next-step panel.

## Imagery and icons

- Use authentic, consented photographs of residents, organizers, public spaces, facilities, workshops, gardens, and neighborhood activity.
- Favor natural light, visible local context, multigenerational interaction, and documentary composition. Images should show participation rather than staged civic symbolism.
- Use one dominant image on the cover and rely on maps, plans, and data exhibits on the remaining pages.
- Maps should be schematic and readable, with only the streets, sites, route, and orientation needed for the proposal.
- Icons are optional. When used, choose one simple solid or line family and keep them secondary to labels and evidence.
- Do not use generic city skylines, handshake stock, political campaign imagery, or AI-generated residents as evidence of community support.

## Avoid

- Do not make the proposal look like a luxury property brochure, a corporate ESG report, or a government form.
- Do not use glossy effects, gradients, heavy shadows, oversized rounded cards, decorative blobs, or dense icon grids.
- Do not invent resident quotes, survey findings, partner commitments, funding, approvals, dates, or achieved impact.
- Do not present one photograph or anecdote as proof of broad community support.
- Do not overload maps with street detail or timelines with unreadable administrative tasks.
- Do not hide exclusions, maintenance responsibility, access requirements, or measurement limitations in tiny text.
- Do not use vague participation language; every call to action should state who can join, what they will do, when, and what support is available.
